---
title: "Network Interfaces"
---

A **network interface** is the kernel's name for a connection point between your computer and a network. Your apps never talk to hardware directly. They hand data to the kernel, and the kernel sends it out through an interface.

Think of the computer as a hospital building. The **kernel's network stack** is the mail room. **Interfaces** are the doors: the main entrance, the ambulance bay, an internal corridor. The **routing table** is the mail room's rulebook that decides which door each outgoing letter uses.

```
 ┌──────────────────────── Your Linux machine ────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                     │
 │   Browser      ssh      Python app        ← user space (programs)  │
 │      │          │           │                                       │
 │      └──────────┼───────────┘  sockets                              │
 │                 ▼                                                   │
 │      ┌─────────────────────────────┐                                │
 │      │  Kernel network stack       │  ← "mail room"                 │
 │      │  (TCP/IP + routing table)   │                                │
 │      └──────┬─────────┬─────────┬──┘                                │
 │             │         │         │                                   │
 │          [ lo ]   [ enp3s0 ] [ wlp2s0 ]  ← interfaces ("doors")     │
 │             │         │         │                                   │
 └─────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼───────────────────────────────────┘
               │         │         │
          (loops back  Ethernet   Wi-Fi
           to itself)   cable     radio
```

Every interface has a few properties:

| Property | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Name | How you refer to it | `enp3s0`, `lo`, `docker0` |
| State | Up or down | `UP` |
| MAC address | Hardware (Layer 2) address, if any | `3c:7c:3f:1a:2b:4c` |
| IP address(es) | Layer 3 address(es) | `192.168.1.50/24` |
| MTU | Largest packet size it will send | `1500` bytes |

## Physical vs. virtual interfaces

An interface does **not** have to be a real piece of hardware. The kernel treats both kinds the same way, which is what makes Linux networking so flexible.

```
                     Network interfaces
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
          │                                   │
      PHYSICAL                             VIRTUAL
   (backed by hardware)              (created by software)
          │                                   │
   ├─ enp3s0  Ethernet NIC            ├─ lo          loopback (127.0.0.1)
   └─ wlp2s0  Wi-Fi card              ├─ docker0     Docker bridge
                                      ├─ veth…       container "cables"
                                      ├─ br0         software bridge
                                      └─ wg0         WireGuard VPN tunnel
```

A virtual interface is a full citizen: it has a name, a state, addresses, and an MTU, and the routing table can point traffic at it exactly as it would at a physical card. The difference is only in what sits on the far side.

**About the names.** Modern Linux uses "predictable" names that encode where the device is:

```
  en  p3  s0            wl  p2  s0
  │   │   │             │   │   │
  │   │   └ slot 0      │   │   └ slot 0
  │   └ PCI bus 3       │   └ PCI bus 2
  └ Ethernet            └ Wireless LAN
```

Older systems used `eth0` and `wlan0`, which you'll still see in tutorials and cloud VMs.

## Looking at interfaces on Linux

The modern tool is `ip`, from the `iproute2` package. (`ifconfig` is the older tool.)

```bash
ip link            # list interfaces (Layer 2 view: state, MAC, MTU)
ip addr            # interfaces + IP addresses  (short: ip a)
ip route           # the main routing table
```

Here is example output of `ip addr`, with notes:

```
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 ...
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo              ← talks only to itself

2: enp3s0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ... state UP
    link/ether 3c:7c:3f:1a:2b:4c                ← real MAC address
    inet 192.168.1.50/24 ... dynamic enp3s0     ← LAN IP from your router (DHCP)

3: docker0: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500 ... state DOWN
    link/ether 02:42:1f:8c:3d:9a                ← MAC, but a made-up one
    inet 172.17.0.1/16 scope global docker0     ← the bridge's own address
```

Reading the flags is most of the skill. `UP` means the admin enabled it; `LOWER_UP` means the physical layer is actually live (cable plugged in, radio associated). `docker0` here is `UP` but has `NO-CARRIER` and `state DOWN`, which simply means no container is attached yet.

## TUN and TAP devices

Some virtual interfaces have a user-space program on the far side instead of a wire. These are **TUN** and **TAP** devices, and they are the mechanism behind almost every VPN on Linux.

A physical interface's other end is a **wire or radio**. A TUN interface's other end is a **program**. When the kernel sends a packet out through a TUN interface, nothing goes onto a cable. Instead, the packet is handed to the program that owns the device, and that program can do whatever it likes with it — encrypt it, tunnel it, log it, drop it.

```
   Normal NIC                          TUN device
   ──────────                          ──────────
   kernel                              kernel
     │                                   │
   [enp3s0]                            [tun]
     │                                   │
   driver → cable                      a user-space program
                                       reads/writes raw IP packets
```

There are two flavors:

| Type | Carries | Layer | Has MAC? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TUN** | IP packets | Layer 3 | No |
| **TAP** | Ethernet frames | Layer 2 | Yes |

A TUN device works at the IP level, so it needs no MAC address and no ARP. In `ip addr` output that shows up as `link/none` and a `NOARP` flag — a reliable sign that you are looking at a tunnel rather than a card.

## How the kernel picks an interface

An interface is only half the story. The **routing table** is what decides which door a given packet leaves by.

```bash
ip route                  # the main table
ip route get 8.8.8.8      # "which door would this packet actually use?"
```

```
default via 192.168.1.1 dev enp3s0 proto dhcp  ← anything not matched below
192.168.1.0/24 dev enp3s0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.50
172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.1
```

Most specific prefix wins, and `default` is the fallback. `ip route get` is the command worth remembering: rather than making you simulate the rules in your head, it asks the kernel to decide and tells you the answer.

Linux can also keep **several** routing tables and consult them in order, via `ip rule`. That is how VPNs divert a slice of traffic without disturbing the main table — the subject of the next chapter.

## Hands-on exercises

```bash
# Inventory
ip link                           # every interface and its state
ip -br addr                       # -br = brief, one line each; good for scanning
ip -d link show docker0           # -d shows the device *kind* (bridge, tun, veth…)

# Which door?
ip route
ip route get 8.8.8.8              # out the default route
ip route get 127.0.0.1            # out lo
ip route get 192.168.1.99         # a LAN neighbour: no gateway needed

# Watch an interface carry traffic
sudo tcpdump -i lo icmp           # terminal 1
ping -c 3 127.0.0.1               # terminal 2
```

Try `ip -br addr` first. The brief view is the one you will actually use day to day; the full output is for when something is wrong.

---

**Summary:** A network interface is a kernel "door" for network traffic. It can be physical (`enp3s0`, `wlp2s0`) or virtual (`lo`, `docker0`, `wg0`), and the kernel treats both the same. A TUN device is a virtual interface whose far side is a user-space program rather than a wire, which is what lets a VPN encrypt packets in transit. The routing table, not the interface, decides which door each packet uses.

The next chapter follows a single TUN interface — `tailscale0` — through a real packet, to see all of this working together.
